#9735. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9734. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

Get more tips for holiday success in our Thanksgiving Baking Guide.

#9732. How to export a ChatGPT conversation (Markdown, PDF and more)

Posted on Nov 8 • Edited on Nov 8 • Originally published at chatgrab.netlify.app

You had a great conversation with ChatGPT: a working script, a plan, a long explanation you'll want again next month. Now you want it out of the chat window and into a file you control.

There are five ways to do it. They differ a lot in what you get back.

Where: Settings → Data controls → Export data.

ChatGPT emails you a link to a zip with all of your conversations, as a chat.html file and a conversations.json file.

Good for: backups. If you want an archive of everything, this is the official way.

Not good for: saving one chat. You get every conversation in one big file, the email can take a while to arrive, and the HTML isn't something you'd paste into notes or share.

Every ChatGPT reply has a copy button under it. It copies that one answer as Markdown, which is handy for grabbing a single code snippet.

Not good for: whole conversations. You copy one message at a time, and your own questions aren't included, so the context is lost.

Selecting the page and pasting it into a document works in a pinch. Expect to clean up: code blocks lose their language, tables often turn into loose lines of text, math shows up twice (once as formula, once as rendered text), and buttons like "Copy code" end up in the middle of your text.

Press Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on a Mac) and choose Save as PDF. This works for short chats. On long ones the sidebar and input box often get printed too, and code blocks can be cut off at the page edge.

Browser extensions read the conversation from the page and rebuild it as a clean file. This is the option to use when you want one chat, formatted properly, in a few seconds.

We built ChatGrab for this. Open a chat, click the icon, and choose:

It works the same way on Claude and Gemini, and everything happens inside your browser. The conversation is never uploaded anywhere.

If you keep notes in Obsidian, turn on frontmatter when exporting. Each file then starts with the title, source, original link and date, so you can search and sort your saved chats like any other note.

#9731. iOS Startup Performance in Practice, Part 2: Measuring App Launch Time in Production

How to measure startup on real user devices, define trustworthy production percentiles, and use XCTest and Instruments to explain regressions.

The easiest way to measure app launch time is to start a stopwatch, open the app, and write down the number.

It is also one of the easiest ways to produce a measurement that cannot be reproduced, compared, or trusted.

An iOS launch depends on more than the code in the repository. The result changes with the process state, system caches, device model, thermal state, available memory, network behavior, stored user data, app version, and the destination the user is trying to open. Two measurements can both be technically correct while describing different experiences.

In Part 1, we separated cold launch, warm launch, resume, scene creation, and entry points. We also defined three possible endpoints: First Draw, Meaningful Content, and Time to Interactive.

Now we can turn that model into a measurement system.

This article is the second part of iOS Startup Performance in Practice, a six-part series:

The goal of this part is not to find a single perfect number. It is to build a production measurement system that describes what real users experience - and then use controlled tests and profiling to explain why that distribution changes.

Suppose one engineer reports a launch time of 1.4 seconds and another reports 2.1 seconds. Before comparing them, we need to know:

Without these answers, the numbers are labels rather than evidence.

Let’s start with production metrics. For every launch metric, define a measurement contract:

Real user launches of app version `8.24.0`

New-process launch; resume reported separately

Icon, link, notification, and quick action segmented where custom telemetry allows it

System launch start for MetricKit; first application marker for custom metrics

First Draw for the system metric; Home Interactive for the product metric

Signed-out and authenticated users reported separately

Device performance tier, iOS version, app version, and migration state

Seven complete days after the target rollout reaches a stable cohort

MetricKit or Organizer for system launch; custom telemetry for product milestones

Internal builds, synthetic runs, invalid or incomplete milestone sequences

This table describes measurement on user devices. There are no fixed test phones, stubbed networks, or XCTest iterations in the production contract. Real device and network diversity are not noise to remove; they are part of the experience we are trying to understand.

The first rule of launch measurement is therefore:

Define the population and user-visible endpoint before naming the number.

Instead of writing “launch time is 1.8 seconds,” write:

For production new-process launches of version 8.24.x, Time to First Draw is 1.1 seconds at p50 and 1.8 seconds at p90 across 2.4 million samples. Authenticated users on the lowest device tier have a p90 of 2.6 seconds.

The values are illustrative, but the form is important: it tells us who experienced the delay, which boundary was measured, and whether the percentile is statistically meaningful.

There is a fundamental limitation in iOS startup measurement:

This means one production number cannot answer every startup question.

Use Xcode Organizer or MetricKit to understand the system-observed launch distribution. These sources can describe Time to First Draw, optimized launch behavior influenced by prewarming, resume duration, and extended launch measurements supported by the OS version.

This is the authoritative source for questions such as:

Use lightweight custom telemetry for milestones the operating system cannot infer:

This is the authoritative source for questions such as:

Do not present an application timer that begins in didFinishLaunching as full launch time. Name it by its actual boundaries, for example AppCodeToHomeInteractive or RouteReceivedToDestinationInteractive.

Together, the two clocks give us a useful production model:

System launch distribution and device/OS trends

Entry-point-specific Meaningful Content and TTI

Instruments, XCTest, Xcode Organizer, MetricKit, and custom telemetry do not compete with one another. They answer different questions.

What startup time do real users experience?

Organizer, MetricKit, and production milestone telemetry

How does the distribution change by app version, device, OS, or user state?

Production telemetry segmented by those dimensions

How long until a requested destination becomes useful?

Which application service delays startup?

Separate resume metric and lifecycle instrumentation

A common mistake is to use the most convenient tool and then reformulate the problem so that it aligns with the result obtained using that tool.

How long does this scenario take under defined conditions?

These activities form a loop, but they should not be confused:

Instruments collects thread states, samples, stack traces, allocations, signposts, and launch phases. That visibility has a cost. Apple explicitly demonstrates that CPU time and wall-clock time in an instrumented trace can differ because profiling itself introduces overhead. It makes Instruments a diagnostic tool rather than the final stopwatch.

Use production data to discover and quantify the problem. Use Instruments to explain its root causes. Use XCTest to make the reproduction scenario repeatable and protect the issue from returning. Then, refer back to production data to verify the result.

As soon as production data reveals which cohort or user journey is performing slowly, create a benchmark that reproduces the situation. This serves as a tool for diagnosing and preventing regressions, rather than as a primary description of the user experience.

Launch tests are sensitive to the state of the whole device. A useful benchmark removes unrelated variance while preserving the characteristic that made the production cohort slow: device class, data volume, migration state, authentication path, or entry point.

The simulator is useful for development, lifecycle experiments, and fast feedback. It is not a reliable representation of iPhone launch performance because it runs on Mac hardware, shares host resources, and does not reproduce the same storage, memory, thermal, scheduling, and rendering environment.

Use physical devices for performance conclusions.

The minimum useful device set normally includes:

Do not compare an “after” result from a new phone with a “before” result from an old one.

Measure a Release configuration, or a dedicated Performance configuration derived from Release.

Avoid drawing conclusions from a Debug build. Debugger attachment, assertions, sanitizers, logging, and the absence of compiler optimizations can change both the duration and the shape of launch.

Keep observability enabled, but make it lightweight. Signposts are designed for this purpose; verbose synchronous logging is not.

Do not cool the device only for the “after” measurement. The goal is not to produce the smallest possible number. The goal is to make before and after comparable.

Startup often depends more on user state than teams initially expect.

The fixture should be deterministic. A performance test that uses an account whose data changes every day is not deterministic even if the test code never changes.

The network is part of the user experience, but it is usually a poor dependency for a code-regression benchmark. Latency, DNS, TLS, server load, routing, and radio state can overwhelm a small application-side change.

For local and CI measurements, prefer one of these contracts:

Then validate real network behavior separately in production.

There is no public API that reliably clears every relevant system cache and requests a “true cold launch.” Force-quitting an app and immediately reopening it creates a new process, but the second launch can still benefit from warmed pages and system services.

Apple recommends warm launches for repeatable development measurements because they are more consistent. XCTest also performs a throwaway iteration before recording measured iterations, reducing first-run cache variance.

That does not mean cold launch is unimportant. It means it needs a different strategy.

Use warm launches for high-signal regression detection:

Evaluate cold behavior through a combination of:

Never label “terminate and immediately relaunch five times” as five cold launches. It is five new-process launches under increasingly warm system conditions.

XCTApplicationLaunchMetric provides the most practical automated baseline for application launch.

A minimal UI performance test looks like this:

Without an extended launch task, XCTApplicationLaunchMetric() measures to the first frame. XCTest runs the measured block repeatedly and ignores an additional initial iteration used to reduce warm-up variance.

If the requirement is that the first frame is also responsive to input, use:

This waits until the main thread is responsive after the first frame. It is often a better default for products that can technically draw a frame while still blocking user interaction.

The two metrics answer different questions:

First frame, plus any explicitly registered extended launch tasks

XCTApplicationLaunchMetric(waitUntilResponsive: true)

Do not silently switch between them when comparing builds.

Launch arguments and environment variables are useful for choosing deterministic fixtures, but the application must process them carefully.

Do not replace the normal startup architecture with a completely different test-only app. The test should control external variance, not remove the code you intend to measure.

A production application usually needs several launch tests:

Entry-point-specific journeys can be added separately, but remember that the built-in application launch metric ends at a system launch milestone. If the product destination becomes useful later, add an application-owned measurement for that interval.

Xcode performance tests can compare results with an accepted baseline and flag regressions. A baseline is only meaningful for a stable environment.

Do not share one absolute baseline across:

For CI, record the device identity, OS, Xcode version, commit, build configuration, fixture, and raw measurements with every run. If any of those dimensions changes, treat the comparison as a new series until you have evidence that the values remain comparable.

Once the benchmark shows that launch is slow, open the same scenario with the App Launch template in Instruments.

Profile a Release build on the same class of physical device used for measurement.

The App Launch template separates major phases such as:

In the trace, inspect more than the total duration:

Pin the app launch phases, main thread, and relevant worker threads. Add Points of Interest so that application-owned phases appear on the same timeline.

Then form one narrow hypothesis. For example:

The root interface waits synchronously for the complete catalog cache, although the first screen needs only the first page.

Change that behavior, return to the controlled XCTest, and measure again. Do not report the duration of the new Instruments trace as the improvement; report the repeated benchmark under the original contract.

System metrics can tell us when the first frame appears. They cannot infer that a product screen contains meaningful data or that a requested route is ready.

Use OSSignposter to make application phases visible:

A small interval wrapper can keep ownership explicit:

The end marker must represent a real product condition. For a home screen, that may require:

Do not end the interval because a convenient callback fired.

XCTest can record the duration between matching signpost events:

This creates an application-specific benchmark, but it has an important boundary: the signpost cannot begin before application code runs. It measures the application-owned interval, not the full system launch.

Good startup signposts are few, stable, and architectural:

Avoid adding an interval around every function. A trace with hundreds of unstable names becomes harder to compare and expensive to maintain.

Signpost names also become part of the observability contract. Rename them deliberately.

An app can produce a fast first frame and still feel slow.

The system First Draw metric may report approximately one second. The user asked for a product and could not act on it for three and a half seconds.

The problem begins when the first number is presented as the complete user experience.

Define a product milestone for each important entry point:

Requested product visible and primary action enabled

Camera preview active and accepting input

This is also why a universal “startup budget” is insufficient. The system launch budget can be shared, but route execution and destination readiness need their own budgets.

Production launch performance is a distribution across users, devices, operating systems, application states, and entry points. A single average hides the experiences that most need attention.

For production launch data, report at least:

Always segment the distribution before interpreting it. At minimum, compare:

A global p90 can remain unchanged while the p90 on the oldest supported devices regresses by several seconds. It can also appear to improve simply because adoption shifted toward newer devices. Segmentation is part of the metric, not an optional dashboard filter.

Do not use production maximum as a release KPI. In a sufficiently large population, isolated extreme values are expected and may reflect interruptions the application cannot control. Use high percentiles, SLO compliance, and sample count to quantify the tail; use diagnostics to investigate pathological individual cases.

For a controlled test, preserve every raw iteration and report the median, p90, and maximum. A small local dataset answers a different question: whether the scenario is stable enough to reproduce a change.

Suppose ten controlled runs produce these durations in seconds:

The median describes the center, while the p90 and maximum reveal instability that an average would blur. Do not delete the slow runs merely because they are inconvenient. Investigate whether they came from the application or from a documented failure of the experiment.

Ten local runs can provide quick feedback, but they do not make a production-quality p99. High percentiles require many samples.

Do not compare a p90 from ten local launches with a p90 from millions of production launches as though they were the same experiment.

Production data is the primary description of startup quality. Controlled tests answer whether a code change affected a reproducible scenario, but they cannot represent every real user.

Xcode Organizer aggregates launch performance from users who share diagnostics and allows teams to compare distributions across app versions and devices. It is the fastest way to establish a system-level production baseline before building any custom pipeline.

MetricKit reports include histogrammed launch and resume information rather than one application-wide scalar. Depending on the OS and SDK generation, launch data includes time-to-first-draw, optimized time-to-first-draw for prewarmed launches, resume time, and extended launch measurements.

Apple is evolving MetricKit toward the newer MetricManager, MetricReport, and typed MetricResult APIs in upcoming SDKs. If you adopt those APIs, isolate the SDK-specific ingestion layer. The measurement model should remain stable even when the transport type changes:

Do not upload a daily payload and discard its dimensions. At minimum, preserve:

Aggregating everything into one average makes regressions on older devices almost invisible.

System metrics understand launch and rendering. They do not automatically know that the product card requested by a notification is ready for purchase.

Avoid including raw URLs, notification payloads, user identifiers, search text, or product data unless the analytics design explicitly requires and permits them. The useful dimensions are normally categories, not content.

Startup observability runs on the critical path, so its design matters.

A lightweight custom recorder might look like this:

Even this code starts only after application code exists. It must never be described as measuring the full interval from the user tap.

The following protocol is a useful starting point for a production team. It begins with user devices and introduces laboratory measurements only after the production metric identifies a problem.

Select the launch scenarios that represent meaningful user traffic and risk:

Keep launch and resume in separate series.

Before creating test fixtures, define the production segments needed to explain the journey: app version, device tier, OS, authentication state, entry-point category, and migration state. Do not collect dimensions that have no analytical purpose.

Use Organizer or MetricKit for system launch and resume distributions. Add lightweight custom milestones for Meaningful Content and Time to Interactive. Buffer and upload the data outside the launch critical path.

Collect a complete, stable rollout window. Report p50, p90, p95, sample count, SLO compliance, and the important segments. Treat resume as a separate metric.

Determine whether the regression belongs to a device tier, OS, app version, entry point, user state, or migration path. This cohort becomes the specification for the controlled experiment.

Choose stable physical devices based on the affected production population. Create deterministic fixtures that reproduce its data volume, authentication state, feature flags, cache state, and network contract.

Use XCTApplicationLaunchMetric for First Draw or responsiveness and signposts for application-owned stages. Use Instruments to connect the slow interval to threads, stacks, dependencies, and launch phases.

Measure after every meaningful change. Once the improvement is reproducible, run the benchmark regularly on fixed hardware and alert on a sustained regression or budget violation rather than one noisy sample.

Compare Organizer, MetricKit, and custom product milestones by app version and the original affected segment. A local win is complete only when the relevant production distribution moves in the expected direction.

A production report should first show the user impact and the affected cohort, then connect it to the controlled experiment used to explain the change:

The exact values above are illustrative. The important property is traceability: the report begins with the real-user regression, identifies the cohort, shows how it was reproduced, and defines how the fix will be validated.

Faster for which scenario, device, endpoint, and percentile?

At this point, the pieces form one system:

Each layer corrects a blind spot in another:

The goal is not to choose one source of truth. It is to know which source is authoritative for each question.

Correct launch measurement begins with real users.

First define the production population, lifecycle path, entry point, start boundary, and meaningful endpoint. Collect enough samples to report p50, p90, p95, SLO compliance, and the device, OS, app-version, and user-state segments that can explain the distribution.

A benchmark tells you whether the code changed. Production telemetry tells you whether the user experience changed.

In Part 3: Finding Bottlenecks from dyld to the First Frame, we will use the measurement system built here to read an App Launch trace phase by phase. We will examine pre-main work, linked frameworks, static initialization, disk I/O, main-thread blocking, rendering, and the difference between CPU time and waiting time.

#9729. Game Renewals: Implement Recurring User Reminders Using Cron and Queues in SaaS Backend

A gaming SaaS reminder is easy to schedule until the business deadline moves, a worker restarts, or the same renewal notice is delivered twice. The simplest design is a database-backed reminder record, one small cron process that claims due work, and a queue whose consumer performs delivery. Keep the cron boundary thin and make recovery a property of the stored state.

TL;DR: store the next delivery time and an explicit attempt state; let cron enqueue a bounded batch; make the worker idempotent; retry with a visible deadline; and reconcile missed work after an outage. A timer is a trigger, not the source of truth. This is the simplest backend shape I would implement for recurring user reminders when recovery matters more than clever scheduling.

For a game subscription, “remind me before renewal” is not one timestamp. It is a business rule with a clock, a timezone, a subscription version, and a delivery policy. A player might receive an email three days before renewal, while a promotional entitlement changes the renewal date tomorrow. If the scheduler stores only a recurring expression, it has no durable answer to the question: which exact reminder is due for which version of the subscription?

I start with one materialized occurrence per reminder. The useful fields are deliberately boring: reminder_id, account_id, subscription_version, due_at, state, attempts, lease_until, and an idempotency key. The row is the audit trail. A cron tick only finds rows whose due_at is in the past and whose state permits work.

I initially assumed a recurring rule was the simpler record. It was the simpler sentence, not the simpler recovery model.

That choice handles a subtle failure mode. If a deadline is edited after a cron expression has been expanded, the scheduler can cancel the old occurrence and create the new one. It does not need to reverse-engineer an old expression or guess which notification a worker was about to send.

The queues are transport mechanisms. The database decides whether a delivery is still valid. That distinction matters during a deploy: a job already in flight may refer to an occurrence that was replaced five seconds earlier. The worker should acknowledge the job after recording a terminal result, while a transient failure should return the occurrence to a retryable state with a future next_attempt_at. In a SaaS backend, that stored decision is more useful than a cron expression that exists only in process memory.

Here is the shape of the decision in Python-like application code. The storage calls are intentionally generic; the important part is the order of checks and state changes.

The five-minute lease above is an example of a bounded claim, not a universal setting. It must exceed the normal critical section and be shorter than the interval in which duplicate work becomes unacceptable. The delivery endpoint also has to honor the same idempotency key, because a worker can lose its connection immediately after the provider accepts a request.

Cron creates a familiar false sense of reliability: a process ran at 09:00, so the reminder must have been handled. That conclusion is unsupported. The process may have read rows and died before publishing; the queue may have accepted a job while the worker was unavailable; or the notification may have been accepted while the result write timed out.

I treat each transition as an operational question:

The awkward case is the middle one: enqueue and database update are two systems, so there is no magical atomicity between them. A durable outbox can narrow that gap, but it adds a table, a publisher, and another recovery loop. For a small reminder feature, a short claim lease plus reconciliation may be easier to operate; for a high-value notification, the outbox cost is justified by the stronger handoff. The trade-off is explicit: this design is not suitable for sub-second scheduling, strict exactly-once side effects, or a workflow whose state cannot be reconstructed from durable records. Those constraints justify a different execution model and more infrastructure.

Do not let reminder payloads become a general-purpose callback system. If an account can configure a URL, validate it against an explicit allowlist or a tightly controlled destination policy, and revalidate at delivery time. Server-side request forgery defenses are a boundary concern, not a scheduling feature; OWASP's guidance covers the distinction between allowlisting and blocking private address ranges, including why the correct choice depends on the application topology.

The useful metrics are about missed business deadlines, not cron uptime alone. Record the age of the oldest due occurrence, claim-to-send latency, retry count, duplicate-suppression count, stale-version cancellations, and the number of occurrences recovered by reconciliation. Alert when the oldest due age approaches the reminder's business tolerance. A green cron process with a growing due backlog is a red system.

Keep the reconciliation job separate from the normal tick. The tick handles a small, predictable batch every minute; reconciliation scans a wider window for pending, expired leases, and retryable occurrences. Bound both scans, order by due_at, and expose the number of rows deferred because the batch limit was reached. Unbounded catch-up after a multi-hour outage can turn recovery into a second outage.

Test the state machine with time fixed and delivery outcomes forced. At minimum, cover a duplicate queue delivery, a worker crash after external acceptance, a changed subscription version, an expired lease, and a missed cron interval. These tests are more valuable than asserting that a scheduler function was called once.

Start by writing occurrences for one reminder type while the existing path remains authoritative. Compare due rows and delivered events, but do not send shadow notifications. Then enable the worker for a small account cohort, with a kill switch that pauses claiming rather than deleting rows. That distinction preserves evidence for recovery.

During migration, keep the old and new idempotency schemes separate or derive one stable key from the occurrence ID; never let both paths independently invent a delivery identity. Once the backlog is empty and the reconciliation metrics are quiet, move ownership of the reminder type, then remove the old trigger only after its last in-flight work has expired.

The decision rule is compact: use cron to wake the system, a durable row to define the work, a queue to absorb execution variance, and an idempotent worker to make retries safe. If the business deadline matters, design the recovery path before adding another scheduling expression.

#9727. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. But it’s not just a stunt: Baking a pie in a paper grocery bag gives you a beautifully golden brown, perfectly cooked pie, with toothsome yet tender apples (which soften better thanks to the steam trapped by the bag) beneath a streusel topping.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

#9725. SolanaGuard AI: Understand Before You Sign

What if you could understand what a Solana transaction is doing before deciding whether to approve it?

That question inspired me to build SolanaGuard AI, an AI-powered Solana transaction security assistant.

I built this project as an individual developer while participating in a Solana hackathon. My goal was to explore how blockchain data and AI could work together to make transaction information easier to understand, especially for people who may not be comfortable reading raw blockchain transaction details.

Interacting with blockchain applications often involves approving transactions without fully understanding what is happening behind the scenes.

A transaction may contain multiple instructions, interact with different programs, or involve changes to token permissions and account authorities.

For experienced developers, inspecting these details may be manageable. For beginners and everyday users, however, understanding what they mean can be difficult.

I wanted to explore a solution that could help users inspect transaction details and understand potential warning signs before making a decision.

SolanaGuard AI allows users to submit a Solana transaction signature for analysis.

The application retrieves transaction information from the Solana Devnet, examines available transaction details, applies deterministic risk checks, and uses AI to explain the findings in plain language.

One important design decision was separating the risk engine from the AI explanation layer.

The risk score is calculated using deterministic rules. AI helps explain the findings; it does not determine or secretly modify the risk score.

This distinction matters because an AI-generated explanation should not be treated as verified blockchain evidence.

I chose Python and FastAPI for the backend because I wanted a straightforward way to retrieve and process transaction data while keeping the application modular.

Building this project was not just about writing code. I also had to understand how the different components communicate.

Retrieving a transaction is only the beginning. Understanding its instructions, accounts, metadata, and token-related information requires careful parsing.

I also had to account for missing metadata, unsupported transaction versions, failed transactions, and RPC errors.

I wanted the application to provide useful warnings without automatically treating unfamiliar programs as malicious.

This meant designing transparent rules and attaching evidence to findings rather than making unsupported security claims.

3. Separating AI explanations from verified facts

AI can make technical information easier to understand, but it can also produce inaccurate explanations.

I designed the system so that deterministic analysis provides the findings and AI helps communicate them. Unknown information should remain unknown rather than being presented as fact.

Getting the application running locally was one milestone. Deploying the backend to Render and preparing the frontend for Vercel introduced another set of challenges.

I encountered a CORS issue while connecting the frontend and backend. Debugging it helped me understand how browser origins, API URLs, and environment variables work together.

These challenges reminded me that building a working application involves much more than getting the code to compile.

This project has helped me understand several important concepts:

I also learned that AI should support security analysis, not replace evidence or create a false sense of security.

I think it is important to be transparent about the limitations.

It is an analysis assistant intended to help users understand available transaction information and identify potential warning signs.

There is still room to improve the project.

Some areas I would like to explore include:

Building SolanaGuard AI has been a valuable learning experience.

As someone exploring the intersection of AI and blockchain development, this project gave me an opportunity to move beyond tutorials and work on a practical problem.

It also reminded me that good AI engineering is not simply about adding an AI API to an application. It is about deciding where AI is useful, where deterministic logic is more appropriate, and how to communicate uncertainty honestly.

I'm looking forward to improving the project and learning from feedback from the Solana and developer communities.

If you're building in the Solana ecosystem or exploring AI-powered security tools, I'd love to hear your thoughts.

#9723. Marketers Are BURNED OUT - And No One Gives AF

I have read countless posts about bloated marketing roles where six jobs are crammed into one title. One listing asked for a “Marketing Manager” to handle brand strategy, paid media, SEO, email marketing, copywriting, and front-end web design. All of that... on a junior salary! These are not rare. They are the norm these days. Scroll LinkedIn or Reddit for five minutes and you will see post after post of people venting about being stretched thin, underpaid, and told to be “grateful for the opportunity.”

I have been reading these for a YEAR now. Watching the same story play out. Marketers are asking, “Is it just me, or has marketing completely lost the plot? Is this the job I wanted? Should I just switch careers?” I even asked the same things myself. I used to love marketing. Now, I don't even know what to say.

What even was marketing before all of this? Was it always like this and we are just noticing it now? Or did it get worse in the last few years?

What used to be a blend of strategy and execution turned into survival mode. AI promised efficiency. Instead, it created more expectation. Faster turnarounds. More output. Tighter budgets. Leadership sees AI as a shortcut, not a tool. So the workload? It went up. Headcount? Went down. Pressure? TRIPLED.

The marketer role did not evolve. It got gutted and repackaged.

This article is not about the trends. Not the hype. Just focusing on the one question we all dread to be answered. How real is marketer burnout, and how did we get here?

What happens when your creative energy gets consumed by meetings, client briefs, and endless edits? How do you stay motivated when everyone blames your team for poor performance but no one credits you when a campaign wins? Why do marketers, especially in digital, feel like they are always running on empty?

Burnout in marketing is not new. What’s different now is how fast it spreads and how deeply it affects people across roles. From content specialists and media buyers to strategists and SEO managers, burnout is everywhere. Not because people are lazy or bad at their jobs. They are overwhelmed, underappreciated, and stuck in systems that demand more while offering less.

Marketers today wear too many hats. Generalist roles stretch across brand, analytics, operations, and sales support. It used to be enough to run great creative. Now you are expected to prove ROI, optimize in real-time, adjust to AI tools, and still produce on-brand messaging across ten platforms. The second something underperforms, marketing takes the fall.

But when results are good? Sales or other department will take the credit. That’s not an exaggeration. One Reddit comment I saw earlier hit it perfectly: “The sales team shouldn't be the only ones getting commission since we (content team) did all the work.” That’s the norm in many agencies and in-house teams.

Marketers drive interest, create value, and nurture leads. Sales closes once the hard part is already done.

There’s a word for that dynamic: exhausting.

Burnout is tied to more than just being busy. It’s the layoffs. The increased cost of living. The consolidation of roles. Managers freeze raises. Employees fear losing their jobs, so they overperform to avoid the next round of cuts. That creates a cycle. You take on more. You work harder. You don’t complain. And then your reward is more responsibility, not more support. Not a better salary.

You become your own bottleneck. You say yes to everything because the team is small and leadership needs “just one more push.” Eventually, you hit a wall. Creativity dies. Enthusiasm fades. Work turns into survival.

Marketing roles are highly visible but rarely respected. Everyone thinks they can do your job. Leadership gives vague direction but expects strong positioning. Product teams shift priorities mid-sprint. Sales wants new decks with impossible turnaround times. People expect you to spin gold out of nonsense with a smile on your face.

Meanwhile, your inbox fills up with subject lines like “quick tweak,” “minor edit,” and “urgent request.” These aren’t minor. They’re entire projects disguised as favors. And they never stop.

This is why boundaries matter. The problem is, setting boundaries gets seen as being “difficult” or “not a team player.” So people stop trying. They take the hits in silence.

A common theme in marketing burnout is the rejection of sales culture. Some marketers say, “I don’t want to do sales. I’m an introvert.” That mindset makes you easy to ignore in corporate environments. One Reddit commenter put it plainly. Marketing is sales. You sell ideas to bosses, value props to clients, and narratives to users. You’re not on the phone closing deals, but you are pitching all the time.

People who thrive in marketing know how to talk. They present data with confidence. They make their case without waiting for approval. They build allies. And yes, sometimes they party with clients to keep them loyal.

The problem is not that marketers don’t work hard. It’s that most of them don’t get taught how to sell themselves. That disconnect builds resentment over time.

Fixing burnout in marketing requires more than taking a week off or downloading a mindfulness app. Companies and leadership need structural change.

1. Credit needs to be shared. If a campaign brings in leads, content, media, and analytics should all get credit. This is not a favor. It’s the truth! Stop handing out bonuses to sales without acknowledging who did the heavy lifting.

2. Boundaries must be normalized. No one should work weekends to chase someone else’s last-minute idea. Make deadlines real. Protect personal time. Normalize saying no.

3. Redefine performance. Measuring success only through ROI creates a narrow path to burnout. Not every channel performs the same way. Not every campaign wins in thirty days. Look at long-term impact, brand growth, and engagement quality.

4. Advocate up the chain. Teach marketers how to pitch. Not just to customers. To leadership. Make the case for headcount, for tools, for strategy. If you don’t make noise, you won’t get noticed.

5. Say the quiet part out loud. Marketers need space to admit when they are tired. When they feel ignored. When they need clarity. Create a culture where people can be honest without fear.

Burnout doesn’t mean you are in the wrong field. It means the structure around you is broken. You shouldn’t need to chase credit. You shouldn’t need to hide exhaustion. You shouldn’t be constantly afraid of layoffs or budget cuts or being replaced by automation.

Good marketing is emotional work. It requires A LOT of creativity, patience, and most importantly clarity. You cannot fake that for long. At some point, your output suffers and your health goes with it.

There is a way forward, but it starts with truth. Stop pretending everything’s fine. Start fixing the real problems.

If your team is burned out, they don’t need a pep talk. They need help. Give them that, or lose them.

Wrote this for every marketer who’s been holding it in.

#9722. Wie Codex CLI eine Aufgabe an einen osFoundry-Agenten, ein Team oder einen Loop übergibt

Am Ende kann Codex CLI Arbeit, die es nicht selbst erledigen sollte, an eine Session in osFoundry abgeben: eine Agent-Session, eine Team-Session oder einen Loop. Es schickt ein Ziel, eine Zusammenfassung dessen, was es schon weiß, und das Ergebnis, das es zurückhaben will. Der Owner der Session bekommt eine Benachrichtigung und klickt auf Accept and run (annehmen und ausführen) oder Decline (ablehnen). Sobald der Run fertig ist, liest Codex das Ergebnis in derselben Terminal-Session und macht weiter. Gibst du ihm stattdessen einen Runner-Platz, kann es selbst einen begrenzten Run starten, ganz ohne Klick.

Klick in osFoundry auf das Schlüsselsymbol in der Kopfzeile und öffne den Tab Connected ("Connected agents"). Unter "Connect in three steps" stellst du Assistant auf Other MCP client, gibst einen Anzeigenamen wie Codex CLI ein und klickst auf Add assistant. Der Owner sieht diesen Namen bei jedem Handoff, also nimm einen, den er wiedererkennt.

Beispiel: Der Tab Connected agents mit einer Codex-CLI-Verbindung

Öffne dann ~/.codex/config.toml und beschränke die Tabelle auf das, was dieser Job braucht:

osfoundry:run ist der Scope hinter request_session_run. Lass ihn weg, wenn Codex immer nur vorschlagen soll. Die Handoff- und Notiz-Tools brauchen osfoundry:write, die drei lesenden osfoundry:read. Mit "writes" fragt Codex vor den vier Tools nach, die nicht als read-only markiert sind, und führt die lesenden ohne Rückfrage aus.

Der Browser öffnet die Seite "Connect an agent" von osFoundry. Mit den Scopes oben zeigt "Requested capabilities" drei Zeilen. Die dritte lautet "Run sessions where you grant a runner role". Wähl den Workspace, dann "Use pending: Codex CLI", setz das Häkchen bei der Bestätigung und klick auf Connect.

Zurück im Tab Connected steht bei der Verbindung "Connected." Unter Projects wählst du das Projekt und klickst auf Add to project. Damit sieht die Verbindung die infrage kommenden Sessions des Projekts. In keine davon darf sie bisher schreiben.

Beispiel: Der Bereich Projects mit einem hinzugefügten Projekt

Weiter unten kommt "Agent, Team, and Loop sessions". Die Hilfezeile sagt schon alles: "Invite it to a session as Contributor to post notes and propose handoffs, or Runner to also request runs. A handoff still needs the session owner's approval."

Beispiel: Der Bereich Agent, Team, and Loop sessions mit Codex CLI als Contributor in einer Team-Session

Die Liste bietet nur Sessions aus Projekten an, zu denen diese Verbindung hinzugefügt wurde. Wähl Typ, Session und Rolle und klick auf Save role. Fang mit Contributor an. Speicherst du später Runner für dieselbe Session, ersetzt das die Rolle.

Auf dem Rechner, auf dem dieser Text entstanden ist, ist Codex nicht installiert, die Session unten ist also ein simuliertes Beispiel. Die Tool- und Argumentnamen sind die, die der Live-Server über tools/list liefert, mit dem Präfix mcp__osfoundry__, das Codex vor MCP-Tools setzt. Repository, Session und alle Werte sind Demo-Inhalte.

Auf der Owner-Seite geht es schnell. Die Benachrichtigung lautet "Codex CLI requests a handoff" mit "Review the request in Release desk." und einem Button Review handoff. Der öffnet den Tab Handoffs der Session. Unter "Outside assistant requests" steht das Ziel in voller Länge, "Context and expected output" lässt sich aufklappen, und die Zeile "Up to 4 rounds on your agent runtime" zeigt, wie viel der Run tun darf. Accept and run stellt ihn in die Warteschlange ("Handoff accepted and run queued"). Decline beendet ihn.

Beispiel: Die Benachrichtigung Codex CLI requests a handoff mit dem Button Review handoff

Beispiel: Eine offene Anfrage eines externen Assistenten im Handoffs-Tab der Session, mit Accept and run und Decline

Hat Codex das Falsche geschickt, zieht cancel_session_handoff mit der handoff_id es zurück, solange der Owner noch nicht angenommen hat.

Vorschlag und Run sind mit Absicht zwei Tools. propose_session_handoff fragt einen Menschen. Es braucht osfoundry:write, einen Contributor-Platz sowie einen für Menschen lesbaren context_summary und requested_output, und nichts startet, bevor der Owner klickt. request_session_run überspringt den Klick. Es braucht osfoundry:run und einen Runner-Platz, den der Owner vorab vergeben hat, der Klick ist also einmal passiert, als der Platz vergeben wurde. Beide begrenzen max_rounds auf 10. Der Vorschlag begrenzt goal auf 5.000 Zeichen, der Run auf 10.000.

Codex sieht Ergebnisse, keine Überlegungen. read_session_task_result liefert nur Tasks, die diese Verbindung gestartet hat. read_session_mail liefert Notizen an die Verbindung und Notizen, die sie selbst gepostet hat, und in der Tool-Beschreibung steht "Internal agent analysis is excluded." post_session_note fügt eine zugeordnete Notiz hinzu, auf die die Agenten der Session antworten können, und sie "does not trigger an automatic run".

Die Session läuft da, wo sie immer läuft. Ein Handoff bringt weder das Modell noch die Keys noch das Repository von Codex nach osFoundry. Er transportiert Text, und die Session arbeitet mit ihren eigenen Agenten und Tools. Alles, was nur lokal auf dem Desktop existiert, etwa ein lokaler Ordner oder ein nicht synchronisiertes Element, bleibt außer Reichweite. Die initialize-Antwort des Servers sagt das auch: "Local-only data is unavailable to cloud clients."

Den Zugriff zu entziehen ist ein Klick. Entfern den Platz im Tab Connected oder widerruf die Verbindung, und der nächste Session-Aufruf von Codex wird abgelehnt.

Für den ersten Versuch eignet sich ein Loop, den du bisher von Hand startest. Lade Codex CLI als Contributor ein, schließ eine Änderung in deinem Repository ab und bitte Codex, den nächsten Run des Loops mit einer Zusammenfassung der Änderungen vorzuschlagen. Handoffs zeigt, wie die osFoundry-eigenen Agenten Kontext zwischen Schritten weitergeben, und Agent Sessions zeigt, wo der Tab Handoffs sitzt.

#9715. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9714. I Built an Interactive 3D Camera You Can Take Apart in Your Browser 📷

I've been exploring Three.js and WebGL lately, experimenting with different ways to make websites more interactive.

One thing I really enjoy about 3D on the web is that you're not limited to displaying objects. You can actually let people interact with them, explore them, and understand how things work.

So I decided to build something around that idea.

Meet Camera Lab — an interactive 3D experience where you can explore a DSLR camera, take it apart, and see what's happening inside.

Instead of simply displaying a 3D camera that rotates, I wanted people to be able to explore the engineering behind it.

One of my favourite parts is the exploded view. Seeing the different components separate and come back together makes the whole experience much more interesting.

The main technologies behind the project are:

The camera model is generated using procedural 3D geometry rather than relying on a downloaded camera model.

This made it possible to work with the components individually and create the interactive disassembly experience.

What interests me most about Three.js is how it opens up a different approach to web development.

A website doesn't always have to be a collection of pages, buttons, and forms.

Projects like this make me want to keep exploring interactive product visualizations, 3D storytelling, and educational experiences on the web.

And honestly, there's still a lot I want to learn.

I'd really appreciate some feedback from fellow developers, especially anyone working with Three.js, WebGL, or creative frontend development.

Live demo: https://the-camera.vercel.app/

GitHub: https://github.com/jude4/the-camera

I'm also thinking about what I could build next using Three.js.

#9710. From SoWa Power Station to the Binding Pocket: Why Structural Biology Needs Its Hallway Moment

I still remember the hum of the SoWa Power Station on a rainy Tuesday in Boston. The old brick building, repurposed into a co‑working space, smelled of cold coffee and solder. I was hunched over a laptop, a half‑finished Dockerfile blinking on the screen, while a colleague across the table wrestled with a Cryo‑EM map that refused to converge. Between sips of lukewarm espresso we talked about the same thing every structural biologist talks about in hallways: the gap between a raw density map and a chemically plausible binding pocket.

That conversation — just a few minutes in a noisy corridor — became the catalyst for a months‑long project that reshaped how my team thinks about model building. The problem isn’t new. AlphaFold2 gave us remarkable backbone predictions, but the side‑chain rotamers in ligand‑binding sites still drift. Cryo‑EM maps at 3 Å often leave the density for a bound fragment ambiguous. And the traditional pipeline — manual fitting in Coot, followed by real‑space refinement in Phenix — feels like stitching a quilt with a needle that keeps slipping.

I decided to treat the pipeline as a software system rather than a series of manual steps. The first architectural decision was to separate data ingestion from model generation. A thin Rust service pulls map files from an S3 bucket, validates voxel spacing, and writes a normalized MRC header into a PostgreSQL table. The schema is deliberately minimal:

Downstream, a Python worker pool (Celery + Redis) consumes rows from that table. Each worker launches a containerized pocket‑finder that runs a deterministic fragment‑placement algorithm: a Monte‑Carlo search guided by a differentiable density‑correlation loss. The loss function is simple enough to be expressed in a few lines of PyTorch, yet it captures the physics we care about:

Because the loss is differentiable, we can back‑propagate through a small equivariant graph neural network that predicts side‑chain chi angles. The network was trained on the PDBbind refined set (≈ 12 k complexes) — no proprietary data, just publicly available structures. Training took 6 hours on a single A100; inference on a 3 Å map finishes in ~45 seconds per ligand.

The engineering trade‑off that surprised me most was the batch size of the Monte‑Carlo sampler. Early prototypes used 10 000 proposals per ligand, which gave a nice smooth convergence curve but blew the GPU memory budget when we tried to run 200 ligands in parallel. Reducing to 2 000 proposals cut memory use by 70 % and only increased the median RMSD of the top‑ranked pose by 0.12 Å — well within the experimental error of the maps we handle. That decision turned a prototype that could process a dozen structures a day into a service that clears a 500‑map queue overnight.

I still hear the echo of that hallway chat when I watch the dashboard. The Prometheus metrics show a steady 98 % success rate for pocket detection, and the Grafana panel for “average wall‑time per ligand” hovers at 1.3 minutes. But the real win isn’t the numbers; it’s the fact that a junior scientist can now push a new Cryo‑EM dataset through the same API that our senior modelers use, get a ranked list of plausible binding modes, and move straight to synthesis planning. The hallway moment became a reproducible, version‑controlled workflow.

There were setbacks. The first time we swapped the Monte‑Carlo sampler for a Hamiltonian Monte‑Carlo implementation, the acceptance rate plummeted to 3 % and the pipeline stalled for two weeks. I remember staring at the logs at 2 am, wondering if the extra gradient evaluations were worth the latency. We reverted, added a simple adaptive step‑size heuristic, and the acceptance rate climbed back to 23 %. The lesson: sometimes a well‑tuned simple algorithm outperforms a theoretically superior one when you have hard latency constraints.

Now, when a new fragment library arrives — say, a 10 k‑compound covalent set — the team only needs to drop a CSV into the ingestion bucket. The same Rust service parses SMILES, generates 3‑D conformers with RDKit, and enqueues them. The pocket‑finder treats each conformer as an independent ligand, and the results are written back to a results table keyed by map_id and ligand_id. Downstream, a Jupyter notebook pulls the top‑5 poses per ligand, computes interaction fingerprints, and feeds them into a SAR model. The whole loop, from map upload to SAR prediction, runs in under an hour for a typical campaign.

What started as a conversation beside a flickering fluorescent light has become a piece of infrastructure that lives in our CI/CD pipeline, versioned alongside the rest of our codebase. The “hallway moment” — that spontaneous, low‑friction exchange of ideas — is now codified as an API contract, a set of container images, and a handful of SQL migrations. It’s reproducible, auditable, and, most importantly, accessible to anyone on the team who can write a curl request.

If you’ve ever stood in a corridor, coffee in hand, wondering why the best ideas only happen when you’re not at your desk, consider turning that moment into a service. The tools are there: container orchestration, differentiable programming, open structural data. The hallway is just a metaphor for a well‑designed interface between people and computation.

Let’s keep the conversation going — share your own hallway‑to‑pipeline stories, and together we’ll build the next generation of structural‑biology tooling.

#9708. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.
