#9642. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9640. TikToker Makes French Onion Soup In The Microwave (We Tried It, It's Legit)

French onion soup is a classic dish that has roots in ancient Roman cuisine and was further developed in France throughout the 1700s. The version we know today has ties to the city of Lyon, but it didn't get its signature toppings of toasted bread and melted cheese until it became popular in Paris. It has since become a bistro favorite and a fixture on American tables. The only problem with the soup is that even a simple recipe requires a lot of time just to caramelize the onions to perfection — around 30 minutes, at least — and one quicker alternative resorts to using a packet of instant soup mix. A TikToker, however, found a middle path that takes around 15 minutes to prepare in total.

Microwaves are efficient at heating liquids, and since raw onions contain almost 90% water, this kitchen appliance can cook them in a fraction of the time it would take on a stovetop. Starting the process in a covered bowl will sweat the onions and conserve their juices while they soften. Finishing the cooking process uncovered then evaporates those juices and allows the onions to brown.

Using beef broth or stock is also one of the best ways to add flavor to this recipe, and heating everything together for a couple of minutes melds the flavors of all the ingredients into a harmonious soup. The use of croutons is also a genius tip that cuts back on the time it would take to slice and toast a baguette. While this recipe looks legit, it almost seems too good to be true, so I decided to test it out for myself.

The beautiful thing about this recipe is that it calls for ingredients you may already have in your kitchen, and when I realized that I didn't have to make a special trip to the supermarket, I knew I had to try it out for myself. I started by slicing half an onion — we recommend using a yellow onion for the best results. Microwaving it covered for three minutes gave me the same results as in the TikTok video. However, things took a turn when I proceeded to cook the onions uncovered.

The TikToker microwaved their onions for two increments of three minutes and 30 seconds and achieved a light caramelization. My onions already reached that level of browning after the first increment of cooking, and after another minute and a half, they began to burn. Since microwave strengths vary, I recommend cooking your onions in much shorter increments to prevent the same unpleasant results. If you really want to cut back on the time and are worried about burning your onions, opt for birista, or South Asian-style crispy fried onions, that don't require cooking.

The other elements of this recipe worked beautifully, though. The addition of Worcestershire sauce added some acidity and umami to balance the deep flavors of the onions. While half a teaspoon of garlic powder may seem like a lot to add to such a small quantity of soup, it actually played well with the onions and added an additional layer of flavor to the mix. The croutons also soaked up the broth without disintegrating into the soup. I used shredded Gruyère cheese for a traditional touch, which added more dimension to the soup, but mozzarella would also work well in this recipe.

#9637. Meatloaf Is So Much Juicier When You Add This Boxed Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you want a meal that sticks to your ribs and brings a measure of comfort with every bite, you want a good, homemade meatloaf, one of America's favorite dinners. It's traditionally made with ground beef, though to keep things tender, people often include ground pork or Italian sausage. Some include a cooked-down vegetable mix to help the loaf stay moist, while others employ the use of milk. But there's a boxed (or bagged) ingredient likely already in your pantry that you might bring out next time you make meatloaf and want to avoid a crumbly, cracking mess, and it'll help create the juiciest version you've likely ever had. Instant mashed potatoes, which are great to keep on hand for soups and sauces, are about to be your secret weapon in the battle against dry meatloaf, too.

Instant mashed potatoes might sound like a strange mix-in, but hear us out. They're dehydrated and flaky, which makes them ideal when used in meatloaf because when those flakes get dampened by your other ingredients (meat, milk, egg), they thicken, adding bulk and binding the mixture together. More importantly, though, these hard-working flakes hold onto moisture, locking it inside the loaf inside instead of letting the juices run out quite so freely, so your dinner won't dry out during its long cook in the oven.

While moist meatloaf is reason enough to add instant mashed potatoes to the mix, there are a few other benefits worth considering. First and foremost: They're cheap, and they keep for a long time. You can typically get a box from Walmart for less than $4 (prices may vary), and its bags often start at just a buck apiece. Many brands can last up to a year, so you can keep them in your pantry, and they'll likely be good to go the next time you're in the mood for meatloaf (or shortcut gnocchi, for that matter).

Furthermore, most instant mashed potatoes are gluten-free. While you'll want to be sure to check the labels before using them, these potato flakes can often make meatloaf accessible to our friends and family with celiac disease or gluten sensitivities, since they can substitute for breadcrumbs.

Finally, a few tips when employing instant spuds in your dinner loaf. You might let them sit for a few minutes after combining them with the other ingredients, before you introduce the meat; this gives them the opportunity to "set up." And you're not confined to just plain buttery instant mashed potatoes. Give your supper a major upgrade with different flavors of boxed flakes, like sour cream and chives, four cheese, and more.

#9636. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9633. Not Butter Or Cheese: The Creamy Ingredient That Makes Grilled Cheese 10x Richer

Grilled cheese is already a decadent meal that requires little effort, but a different form of richness from meat, rather than cheese, can make it more complexly delicious. If you're going to reach for rich meat, then look no further than pâté, something that comes in enough variety to suit any cheese combination you choose for your sandwich.

Many of us are familiar with pâté on a charcuterie board, served with a light cracker so you can experience its full flavors. But it's a common sandwich ingredient — take, for example, French influence in the Vietnamese bánh mì, creating an international grilled cheese style that's as unique as it is delicious. As it heats, the pâté practically melts like a meaty butter, infusing your cheese and bread with all that richness and delivering a truly powerful taste. When done properly, the pâté should mix directly into the gooey cheese, creating a single filling with the best possible texture.

Thanks to its high fat content, pâté has a signature silky texture that's hard to find elsewhere. Even vegetarian varieties made from mushrooms, soft cheese like ricotta, and butter can be a spot of decadence on an otherwise straightforward meal. It has a remarkable capacity for taking even the most underrated cheeses and turning them into gooey perfection, even if they don't have much moisture or fat to begin with. Combined with a sturdy bread toasted with butter or mayo, each layer of your grilled cheese will end up impossibly rich.

Pâté is an extraordinarily delicate ingredient, so adding it to any hot recipe takes a bit of know-how. Some are designed to be eaten hot or cold, so selecting the right variety and application can prevent you from losing out on any of its delicious virtues. For example, a terrine — not to be confused with true pâté or even rillettes — warms beautifully.

Heating up a pâté made to be eaten cold may make it greasy and fall apart, rather than melt. Instead of these, look for ones used in pâté en croûte, a type of fluffy pastry that uses it as a filling. Just like a country variety, aka terrine, it has a coarser texture that adds a satisfying bite to your sandwich and won't split once heated. These can also come in a dizzying variety, from meaty ones seasoned with nothing but salt to ones laden with chopped vegetables, nuts, and spices.

A simple smear on one side of your bread does the trick just fine, and the direct contact with the bread lets it soak up excess fat as it heats. But if you use an aged or low-fat cheese, try incorporating it with another simple trick for a meltier result: grating the cheese first. By tossing the cheese with your pâté, you coat each individual strand with a bit of the fat and ensure that, when they melt, the two ingredients fuse together. If you use slices, it can also help to smear a bit of pâté on each one before layering them between your bread.

#9631. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9628. Grab This Packet Of Seasoning To Transform Store-Bought Snacks Into A Delicious Masterpiece

Many kitchens contain a well-stocked, if not cluttered, spice cabinet, making it easy to grab what you need when a recipe calls for spices. However, don't rule out using those jarred seasonings with store-bought snacks, too — taco seasoning is one such ideal candidate.

This savory spice blend is one of the kitchen's most versatile, useful in everything from elevating your grilled burgers to giving chicken tenders a delicious twist. Bringing together flavors like earthy ground cumin, sweet paprika, onion and chili powders, oregano, salt, and more, it's a testament to the idea that a good spice blend is greater than the sum of its parts. All the more reason to throw it on your favorite snack. Think the crunchy classics: Chex Mix, fresh or bagged popcorn, pretzels, a nut mix, or good ol' chips.

To make sure the seasoning sticks, you'll want to apply some heat and fat, not just sprinkle on the spices. Fold a packet into some tasty melted butter or coconut oil, then mix it into your snack of choice. Bake at around 350 degrees Fahrenheit, stirring occasionally, until you have a delectably browned and seasoned snack mix.

Seasonings are made for modifications. So if a simple dusting of taco seasoning isn't what you're craving, it's easy to fine-tune the flavors to your liking. An easy starting point is a sweet element — honey, agave syrup, or even maple syrup all pair fabulously with taco seasoning. Simply mix the sugary ingredient into the fat to lend the spiced mix an added dimension.

Alternatively, customize the flavors by mixing up the spice blend yourself. Taco seasoning can contain a variety of ingredients in numerous styles, so brighten up your snack seasoning with grated lime zest, or turn up the heat with cayenne or ground árbol chilies. Consider even amplifying the warmth with cinnamon or allspice — ingredients that'll pair terrifically with sweet flavors.

Alongside such reworked blends, keep expanding your store-bought snack repertoire. Throw in a bag of dry-roasted edamame beans, some Fritos, or plantain chips, or buy some chicharrones (fried pork rinds). Mix and match nibbles to your liking, dust with taco seasoning, then enjoy a new world of snackable possibilities.

#9623. New book explores how Ukraine’s artists are shaping the memory of war

Cover illustration by Kyiv-based Ukrainian artist Sergiy Maidukov

As the war grinds on in Ukraine, almost five years after Russia’s full-scale invasion, The Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins reminds us in her timely and sobering new book how artists and writers register the human cost of the conflict.

“The argument of this book is that the literature and art made by these people, some of whom have lost their lives, will shape the war’s memory,” Higgins boldly asserts. Artists, writers, poets and filmmakers are her vital and sympathetic touchstones across cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv and Lviv.

“When a friend, the defence and security editor of The Guardian, suggested I might think about going to Ukraine, I agreed immediately that it was a good idea,” she writes. “I said it lightly, impulsively, and without realising that going there would change me.”

This odyssey begins in the autumn of 2022, encompassing three years of reporting trips to Ukraine. The arc of the narrative is epic and emotional, from arriving in Kyiv on a bright, beautiful day (10 October) to a final documentary account of the destruction of Bakhmut in the east, where an elderly lady called Nina surveys streets blitzed by shell holes that “were once perfectly ordinary”.

Along the way, Higgins deftly interweaves personal milestones such as slowly grasping the Ukrainian language—who knew “verbs of motion” could be so onerous?—detailing how “the war leaked into every [language] lesson”. Dealing with the anger felt by Ukrainians facing “the outrage of violence” is another test for the author, who anchors her account by observing the impact of Ukrainian art and artists, both historic and contemporary.

As testament to the violence and destruction, Higgins draws on a film by the Kharkiv artists Daniil Revkovskyi and Andrii Rachynskyi shown in the Ukrainian pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale. Civilians. Invasion (2023) is an hour-long collage of unedited videos found online that mirror the true reality of constant bombs and bullets.

Higgins’s survey of artists is essential as a journal of record, bringing to the fore figures such as Marharyta Polovinko, whose macabre, penetrating drawings of roaming monsters can be set, Higgins argues, alongside the work of Spanish artist Francisco Goya—famed for The Disasters of War (1810-20)—or the First World War and Weimar imagery of the German painter Otto Dix. Immortalising these creative figures, who may go unnoticed outside Ukraine, is a significant commemorative act (Polovinko was killed in action in 2025, aged 31).

A trained classicist, Higgins frames the events and trauma of the war through Greek mythology. She likens the character of Cassandra—who was condemned to prophesy only the truth but never be believed—to “resolute Ukrainian women, eloquent and truth-telling”, neatly segueing into one of Ukraine’s greatest works of literature, a seminal poem written by Lesya Ukrainka around 1907 (Cassandra: A Dramatic Poem).

Victoria Amelina, a Ukrainian novelist and war crimes investigator who died aged 37 in July 2023 from severe injuries sustained during a Russian missile strike, is one of these “Pale Cassandras”. Amelina was instrumental in bringing to light the buried journal of the late writer Volodymyr Vakulenko who documented life under occupation.

In commemorating friends and colleagues like Amelina, Higgins is searing and eloquent. “[…] grief leaked out of me,” she says, “and I felt like a vessel with no shape, porous, lacking capacity to hold anything.” Such frank admissions could jar but in shaping a war’s memory, this narrative benefits from such measured, personal interludes.

Cultural erasure is a weapon of war: at least 120 Ukrainian museums have been damaged in the conflict, according to the country’s culture ministry. Russian president Vladimir Putin is not only attempting to annihilate the military and political leadership, but also its cultural warriors in a ruthless bid to vanquish the existence of a sovereign Ukraine. Higgins’s book is a bulwark against this campaign; as a personal memoir it is deeply affecting, and as a journalistic record it is transformative.

• Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, by Charlotte Higgins, published by Jonathan Cape, 272pp, £22 (hb), 20 August

#9621. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9606. New book charts American artist’s lifelong devotion to the South Seas

Robert Lee Eskridge’s Stone-Fishing (around 1930) shows the Polynesian fishing practice of using ropes and stones Courtesy of www.GalleryHawaiiana.com

This is a book about a love affair, one that ran so deep it yielded thousands of watercolours, hundreds of oil paintings and three illustrated books. The painter Robert Lee Eskridge (1891-1975) first visited the South Seas in May 1927, when his ship pulled into the harbour of Papeete, Tahiti. Seeking respite from the grey skies and bone-chilling winters of Chicago, he was instantly smitten and kept returning to the South Seas, eventually making his home in Honolulu, Hawai’i.

Little in Eskridge’s early life had predicted that infatuation. Born in Philadelphia, he attended the Art Institute of Chicago, studied in Paris with the Cubist painter André Lhote, and travelled across Europe for three years. His style, fusing Art Deco patterns with a form of relaxed realism, won him gigs as an illustrator and artist, culminating in a high-profile commission to produce murals for the lobby of the newly rebuilt Palmer House hotel in Chicago. On the eve of his departure for Tahiti, he chose Marco Polo as his subject. (The murals were painted over in 1966.)

Falling in love with the South Seas is not a unique experience. Names like Herman Melville, Robert Louis Stevenson and Paul Gauguin conjure lush tropical forests, foam-crested waves lapping pristine beaches, and carefree Islanders performing hula dances: a vision inevitably darkened by the damages wrought by colonialism. The Islanders Eskridge painted, unlike Gauguin’s, are not immobilised by the artist’s desire to project meaning into them. They are walking, working, dancing, fishing and making music, living fully in the present even as they honour their rich traditions.

Eskridge’s enthusiasm for Islander culture finds a perfect match in biographer Cook’s enthusiasm for Eskridge. While the more lyrically effusive passages in this volume might not appeal to everyone, the lavish illustrations drawn from multiple collections and the excellent captions help us understand the breadth, range and sophistication of a supremely adaptable painter who deserves to be better known. (Regrettably, some images—of the lost Chicago murals, for example—are AI-produced).

Eskridge’s paintings, whether they show bustling street scenes or re-create rituals he witnessed, vibrate with life. As a young man, he was entranced with Sandro Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (around 1485, in the Uffizi Gallery), and that painting’s revelatory spirit lingers on in Eskridge’s bright, luminous colours or in the way he arranges groups of people around a central figure or an activity.

His training under Lhote shapes the cascading abstract forms Eskridge uses in the background of works such as Stone Fishing (around 1930, Gallery Hawaiiana). In this ancient Polynesian fishing practice, men use ropes with stones to herd leaping fish into shallower waters—a communal effort as well as an occasion for individual daring, represented here beautifully by the young man in the middle, who jumps to grab a fish from the air. A later masterpiece is Hilo Wharf (around 1949, Honolulu Museum of Art), a harbour scene, in which Eskridge blends shirtless workers and the bodies of gigantic tuna fish, some already packed up, into an intense drama of shapes, colour and movement.

Since Eskridge treated the Islanders and their culture with respect, they accepted him as one of their own, Cook tells us. They even asked Eskridge to represent them at the Chicago World’s Fair in 1933. Invitations followed to provide Hawaiian-themed murals for the McCoy Pavilion in Honolulu’s Ala Moana Park and, later, to design clothes for the Hawai’ian label Paradise Sportswear.

Always one to defy expectations, Eskridge, at age 64, married Helen Gebhardt and settled in Olympia, Washington. But the Islands kept calling. He died in April 1975 at a hotel in Honolulu named, appropriately, Hale-kulani, “house befitting heaven”.

• C.J. Cook, Robert Lee Eskridge, South Pacific Dreams Publishing, 344pp, 509 col. illust., $59.95 (hb), published 11 August

• Christoph Irmscher is a critic and biographer

#9602. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9601. Underappreciated artists from the Chelsea Hotel are finally getting their due

Bettina standing outside of the Chelsea Hotel, New York Courtesy the artist’s estate

Since its opening in 1884, New York’s Hotel Chelsea has been famed as a hotbed of creativity—a seedy yet alluring beacon drawing artists, musicians and bohemians of all kinds. While the luminaries associated with the place (Mark Twain, Janis Joplin, Andy Warhol) are well known, less famous residents are only now beginning to gain recognition.

Among the more recently “discovered” artists who once called the Chelsea home are the late Bettina (1927-2021), Ching Ho Cheng (1946-89), Bernard Childs (1910-85), Herbert Gentry (1919-2003), Nicola L. (1932-2018) and Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020). Many of their relatives still live in the building; some feel their presence to this day.

“It’s happened many times, Ching contacting me,” Cheng’s sister, Sybao Cheng-Wilson, tells The Art Newspaper. She moved into the Chelsea in the 1980s to take care of her brother, who was dying of Aids. For years after Cheng’s death, the bathroom light bulb would flicker on his birthday, 26 December; Cheng-Wilson became convinced it was his way of checking in on her.

For her part, Cheng-Wilson became dedicated to preserving her brother’s legacy. She held onto both his art and the apartment where he made it. She even raised her daughter at the Chelsea, despite its notorious reputation as a hedonistic haven.

Judith Childs and her artist husband moved into the Chelsea in 1966. “My parents were a little horrified by the whole building,” she recalls. “It was not an elegant hotel.” Childs still lives in the first-floor apartment she and Bernard once shared, surrounded by his soft-hued geometric abstractions that seem to glow from within.

Bernard Childs’s work at the Armory Show 2026 Courtesy Bank

In September, these works—imbued with an almost cosmic fluidity—were the subject of a solo stand at New York’s Armory Show with the Shanghai- and New York-based gallery Bank. The 1970s canvases—priced between $14,000 and $55,000—stood out amid the more than 200 exhibitors at the fair; they hung above a fuzzy, cantaloupe-coloured carpet that enhanced the works’ warm, luminous quality.

Showing an essentially forgotten artist like Childs was a bit of a risk for Bank founder Mathieu Borysevicz. “He’s been off the map for so long,” says the gallerist, who just began working with Childs’s estate. The artist’s work was featured in Documenta in 1959; that same year, he had a solo show at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. But Childs’s previous dealer, Jason McCoy Gallery, last gave the artist an in-person solo show in 2013; the gallery itself closed in 2024.

Borysevicz already had experience helping artists from the storied hotel emerge from the shadows, having worked with the Cheng estate since 2021.

Over Cheng’s short but prolific career, the artist developed four major bodies of work, beginning with psychedelic paintings inspired by Tibetan spiritualism before experimenting with airbrushed gouache, graphite on torn paper and rusted surfaces made using iron and copper oxide on paper. The artist, who appeared in last year’s Sixties Surreal at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art, will have his first major retrospective in September 2027 at the Addison Gallery of American Art in Andover, Massachusetts.

Ching Ho Cheng in his Chelsea Hotel studio in 1985 Courtesy the artist’s estate

Cheng had moved into the Chelsea in 1976, where he befriended Childs. Judith and Cheng-Wilson have stayed close over the years, united by their shared devotion to preserving and promoting their late loved ones’ work. It was Cheng-Wilson who introduced Judith to Borysevicz.

Another friend of Childs, from his time in Paris in the 1950s, was Herbert Gentry—an African American painter known for his jazz-inspired abstractions. He arrived at the hotel in the late 1960s; Gentry’s second wife, the artist Mary Anne Rose, joined him in 1978. She still lives at the Chelsea and now oversees his estate.

“Herbert’s work is so distinctive stylistically, but he was also foundational in bridging what was happening in North America and Europe,” says Gentry’s dealer, Jeffrey Lee of the New York gallery Ryan Lee. By December, the artist will have work simultaneously in museum group shows in Alabama, Germany and Martinique, plus a solo show at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, Sweden.

But not all Hotel Chelsea artists have family members on the premises to safeguard their legacies. When the reclusive Bettina died in 2021, management quickly began clearing out her apartment. The unit was nearly bursting with the conceptual artist’s life’s work, to the point where Bettina slept in a lawn chair in the hallway, as memorably captured in the 2022 documentary Dreaming Walls: Inside the Chelsea Hotel. That would have been the end of the story had Bettina not connected with the Moroccan artist Yto Barrada in her final years.

Barrada fervently believed in the value of Bettina’s work, and its need to be saved from the dumpsters and shared with the world. Before Bettina’s death, Barrada presented the older artist’s sculptures at the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council Arts Center on Governors Island, leading to an appearance in Greater New York 2021 at MoMA PS1. When Bettina died, it was Barrada who saved the contents of her apartment from the trash. The estate, which Barrada oversees with the assistance of Anna McCormick-Goodhart, is now represented by Ulrik in New York; a solo show at the Ruth Foundation for the Arts in Milwaukee closed in April.

One of Bettina’s index cards outlining the details of her unrealised exhibition The Chelsea Hotel: Artists at Work Courtesy the artist’s estate

“There is a lot to sort and sift through, and it leaves wonderful traces of the history of the making of her works, of her travels, of the people in her life—it’s very densely layered,” McCormick-Goodhart says.

In her later years, Bettina—whose work encompasses photography, printmaking, painting, sculpture, textile and commercial design—was known largely for her eccentricities. But she also planned an ambitious, albeit unrealised, exhibition to show her neighbours’ art. A series of typed index cards from the 1980s reveal the artist list and potential venues for The Chelsea Hotel: Artists at Work. The exhibition would have featured the works of Cheng, Childs, Gentry and Rose, among other residents.

Another artist in this heady milieu was Nicola L. A documentary film-maker, who turned her own lens on her home of nearly 30 years for the 2014 film Doors Ajar at the Chelsea Hotel, Nicola L. is best known for her “functional sculptures”—anthropomorphic furniture shaped like a massive foot, the silhouette of a head and other body parts. In a critique of the objectification of women’s bodies, some mimic the female form, but they somehow avoid feeling overly sexualised.

Nicola L. was largely overlooked until London’s Tate Modern included her work in a broader view of international Pop art for its 2015 exhibition The World Goes Pop. Nicola L.’s first institutional solo show took place in 2017 at New York’s SculptureCenter; the London gallery Alison Jacques began representing her estate after the artist’s death in 2018. A retrospective, When the Earth Turned the Other Way, closed earlier this month at Belgium’s Museum of Contemporary Art in Antwerp, and the travelling museum show I Am the Last Woman Object wrapped up a European tour in March.

Installation view of Nicola L.: When the Earth Turned the Other Way, Museum of Contemporary Art, Antwerp, Belgium Courtesy Alison Jacques

Nicola L. was the catalyst behind the Chelsea Hotel residents’ successful fight to keep their apartments after new ownership embarked on an 11-year renovation project to transform the property into a high-end hotel—where rates start at around $500 per night. It was at her urging that the residents banded together to successfully protect their rent-stabilised tenancy.

“The Chelsea was a safe haven for these artists,” says Christophe Lanzenberg, Nicola L.’s son. “The Chelsea allowed them to thrive and stay in New York, instead of getting kicked out of places where rents were coming up.”

Today, there are 42 families still living at the Chelsea. (One artist, Gerald DeCock, is facing eviction at the end of February after 31 years in residence.) Over the years, those remaining have forged tight bonds.

When Childs died, Gentry sent Rose downstairs to keep Judith company. Rose and Nicola L. shared a Long Island City studio for years. As Nicola L.’s health began to decline due to Alzheimer’s, Rose and Judith kept a close watch. They let her sons know when their mother could no longer live alone.

Though its heyday as a refuge for free-spirited artists is long past, the hotel is still deeply connected to its creative history, including artists who checked out decades ago. The lobby, stairwells and hallways are filled with works of art, some said to have been given to the longtime manager Stanley Bard (1934-2017) in lieu of rent. A new Japanese restaurant, Teruko, opened in the basement last year featuring paintings by its namesake, Teruko Yokoi (1924-2020), who lived at the Chelsea from 1957 to 1960, during her marriage to Sam Francis (1923-94).

Teruko Yokoi’s Untitled (1959) will be on offer on Hollis Taggart’s stand at New York’s ADAA Fair in November Courtesy Hollis Taggart

“I was a baby when she was just coming out of art school, juggling having a newborn and continuing to paint. Her studio was actually in the apartment,” says Yokoi’s daughter, Kayo Malik, who is also a custodian of her estate. But when the couple hosted parties for friends like Mark Rothko and Al Leslie, Francis would have Yokoi put her paintings away, hiding her work.

At the Teruko restaurant, the artist’s pieces are displayed in the dining room, enjoyed and appreciated by guests gathering to share a meal—“a full circle moment”, Malik says. The artist is also the subject of a solo show, Seasons, at New York’s Hollis Taggart (until 25 November). And the gallery is bringing one of Yokoi’s Hotel Chelsea-era works, Untitled (1959), to the ADAA Fair at New York’s Park Avenue Armory (12-16 November); there, it will be on offer at a two-person presentation with the artist Michael West (1908-91). Meanwhile in Los Angeles, the artist has a solo show currently on view at James Fuentes Gallery (until 7 November).

Yokoi eventually moved to Switzerland after separating from Francis. Determined to show her work, she opened two dedicated museums in her native Japan, enjoying a long career across three continents. But Malik still feels close ties to her first home at the Chelsea, that formative chapter in Yokoi’s life, and its vibrant artist community.

“The hotel has had an incredible life,” Malik says.

The influence of New York on the Greek-born artist informs an exhibition designed to fill in the gaps of her story

The five-gallery fair was staged inside one of Manhattan's most famous hotels

The artist’s former residence opens a restaurant named Teruko this month, featuring her works

As a survey on the US artist opens at Tate Modern, there is no shortage of works inspired by his "Combines" at the fair

#9600. 21 Best Cozy Fall Baking Recipes

Apples, pumpkin, and cinnamon everything! Fall baking recipes that are cozy, warm, and delicious.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 10, 2026

Fall baking season is officially here! (The best baking season, to be clear.) There’s no better feeling than a trip to the apple orchard that ends with cinnamon sugar apple cake in the oven, or stocking up on cans of pumpkin knowing that pumpkin muffins are in your future. I LOVE YOU, FALL!

There’s something for breakfast, something for snacking, something for lunchboxes, and something for cozy late-night TV time on the couch. Something for everyone!

Hoping you find some good fall coziness with one of these. Here’s to lots of fall baking! ❤️

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This simple cinnamon sugar apple cake is light and fluffy, loaded with fresh apples, and topped with a crunchy cinnamon sugar layer!

These Apple Muffins are EVERYTHING. Wholesome and nutritious, moist and dense, perfectly but not overly sweet, and honestly divine with a little butter and honey.

Pumpkin muffins are getting a lightly crunchy, sparkly cinnamon sugar topping, and then stuffed to the brim with maple cream cheese whipped cream. YUM.

Pumpkin Granola that is both salty and sweet! Made with REAL PUMPKIN along with oats, coconut, almonds, pistachios, maple syrup, cinnamon, and olive oil. My favorite fall granola! ♡ Adapted from the Last Granola Recipe by my friend The Faux Martha.

These Pumpkin Muffins! Made with oats instead of flour and real maple syrup instead of refined sugar. And everyone loves them, including meeee!

Soft, buttery bites coated in gooey pumpkin caramel sauce and a drizzle of white chocolate. My family loves this pumpkin caramel monkey bread!

Sweet Cinnamon Rolls! Made with pillowy brioche dough and cinnamon sugar tucked into every nook and cranny. This makes a BIG batch of dough that you can divide and save for later…or make extra all for yourself!

Maple Quinoa Granola! Golden, crunchy, naturally sweetened clustery granola with speckles of quinoa, nuts, coconut, oats, chia, and other delicious, good-for-you things!

Browned butter and brown sugar caramelly goodness, crispy edges, barely thick and soft centers, and melty little puddles of chocolate chips.

These layered bars are so simple! Loaded with homemade caramel and apples. Caramely apple layer tucked in by a brown sugar-y crust on both sides.

Five Minute Single Serving Apple Crisp with a wholesome oat, pecan, and coconut oil topping. Made super fast in the microwave! No oven required.

Pumpkin Biscuits with Cinnamon Apples for you! Warm and gooey cinnamon brown sugar apples piled between fluffy pumpkin biscuits that YOU made. Pile on the creamy twists of whipped maple cream cheese and yes, this is exactly the over-the-top brunch/dessert/snack you need.

Pumpkin Energy Bites! The BEST easy fall snack. Made with simple ingredients like oats, pumpkin, almond butter, maple syrup, and pumpkin seeds.

Creamy dulce de leche layered with espresso-soaked ladyfingers in one delightful slice! This Dulce De Leche Tiramisu is my new favorite dessert.

These healthy gingerbread muffins are made with coconut oil, whole wheat flour, and real maple syrup. So puffy and so delicious!

Pumpkin Cake! A perfectly dense, moist cake with a crunchy sweet brown sugar streusel. YUM!

These Healthy Maple Glazed Pumpkin Muffins use whole grains, less oil, and less sugar to make a jumbo fall muffin. Yummm.

These Pecan Pie Energy Bites are a cute lil’ 7-ingredient miracle! Made with dates, pecans, oats, almond butter, and maple syrup, you’re going to be snackin’ on these all. day. long.

This is a recipe for Raisin Bran Muffins from my very best friend. Perfect hot out of the oven with melted butter and honey.

This is an easy, classic, super moist pumpkin bread recipe made with olive oil, pumpkin, and cinnamon, and topped with crunchy turbinado sugar.

Keep the coziness going with a few favorite fall dinners! Comforting, crowd-friendly, and the best meals to make when the weather starts getting chilly.

#9598. Chicken with Cajun Cream Sauce

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – SO cozy! I love this meal!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 17, 2026

This was so so so good! Added into my weekly rotation!! My kids didn’t find it spicy! Big win!

That tomatoey, creamy, shallot-infused gravy is something I haven’t been able to stop thinking about.

I made this dinner for my family on the first barely chilly day a few weeks ago. I think my body had just been waiting for permission to go fall cooking mode, and I just unleashed.

Pan-fried chicken. Luscious, savory Cajun cream sauce. Homemade mashed potatoes. Green beans. Apple crisp for dessert.

I served it in deep bowls and we let the girls eat on the living room floor, using the coffee table as their table, while we watched American Ninja Warrior together with the windows open – which, frankly, is the move of two parents who are feeling extra generous and a little out of their mind with the joys of early fall weather. But that meal will be a top 5 meal for me this year, for sure. We all devoured in silence and then cozied up with full bellies to watch some ridiculous TV together.

Here’s an idea I keep coming back to: shrimp. Like what if you just made the sauce, and then threw a pound of uncooked jumbo shrimp in there? It would poach right in the sauce! I haven’t been able to pull myself away from the chicken and mashed potatoes combination, but I feel shrimp should at least be considered.

Hope this recipe gives you all same cozy fall feelings it gave me.

Also a big fan of using the air fryer here, if you’re not feeling the pan-frying.

This picture shows the shallots minced; I also really love to do this with a thinly sliced shallot, sliced on a mandoline. The shape will give you these little ribbons through the sauce.

Add cream and broth, and simmer till it’s GLORIOUS.

I mean, showstopper material right there.

My favorite combo for serving is mashed potatoes and green beans. LIGHTS OUT. So good.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – loving this easy, cozy weeknight dinner!

To air fry the chicken: Air fry at 375 for 10-12 minutes, or until at least 165 degrees internal temperature.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Oven): Toss 3-4 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt on a sheet pan. Roast the potatoes at 425 for 15 minutes. Scoot the potatoes over, add 3-4 cups broccoli and ¼ cup water to the same sheet pan, and roast for another 15 minutes.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Air Fryer): Toss 2 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt. Air fry at 375 for 12 minutes. Add 2 cups frozen or fresh broccoli; air fry at 400 for another 10-12 minutes.

Keywords: cajun chicken, chicken dinner, mashed potatoes

#9596. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

4. Watson P, Norman SB, Maguen S, Hamblen J. Moral injury in health care workers. Accessed January 4, 2021. https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/moral_injury_hcw.asp

5. Shahrour G, Dardas LA. Acute stress disorder, coping self-efficacy and subsequent psychological distress among nurses amid COVID-19. J Nurs Manag. 2020;28(7):1686-1695. doi:10.1111/jonm.13124

6. Lahav Y. Psychological distress related to COVID-19 — The contribution of continuous traumatic stress. J Affect Disord. 2020;277:129-137. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.141

7. Stovall M, Hansen L, van Ryn M. A critical review: moral injury in nurses in the aftermath of a patient safety incident. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2020;52(3):320-328. doi:10.1111/jnu.12551

8. Pappa S, Ntella V, Giannakas T, Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Katsaounou P. Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and insomnia among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Brain Behav Immun. 2020;88:901-907. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2020.05.026

9. Pietrzak RH, Feingold JH, Feder A, Charney DS, Peccoralo L, Southwick SM, Ripp J. Psychological resilience in frontline health care workers during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;82(1):20l13749. doi:10.4088/JCP.20l13749

10. Krystal JH, Alvarado J, Ball SA, et al. Mobilizing an institutional supportive response for healthcare workers and other staff in the context of COVID-19: the Yale experience. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:12-18. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.11.005

11. Park ER, Sylvia LG, Streck JM, et al. Launching a resiliency group program to assist frontline clinicians in meeting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic: results of a hospital-based systems trial. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:111-112. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.10.005

12. Kameno Y, Hanada A, Asai D, et al. Individual psychotherapy using psychological first aid for frontline nurses at high risk of psychological distress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2021;75(1):25-27. doi:10.1111/pcn.13170.

#9595. 36 Healthy Fall Dinners With All The Cozy

Healthy and nourishing fall dinners that are super cozy, too! Some of my favorite bowls, salads, soups, and more!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 18, 2026

Fall dinners are here, and honestly, this is the kind of food I wait for all year. Steamy bowls, creamy sauces, roasted veggies, cozy spices, and meals that make the whole house smell amazing. These healthy fall recipes bring all the sweater-weather comfort while still being nourishing enough for an everyday weeknight!

To call out a few of my all-time favorites from this list:

Nourishing food should still feel generous, cozy, and completely delicious, and these dinners are it!

Roasted sweet potatoes topped with creamy chipotle sauce, spicy ground chicken, avocado, cilantro, and pickled onion. My family loves them!

I love this Kale Apple Salad! Kale, brussels sprouts, rosemary cashews, apples, fried bread cheese, crispy shallots, and crisp apple maple dressing!

Silky carrot soup topped with spiced ground beef and toasty pine nuts! Bright, savory, warming, all the best things!

Amazingly creamy, saucy chickpea curry served over rice with a dollop of chili crisp and a side of cucumber salad. Ready in 20 minutes!

One of my family’s favorite easy dinners that works SO well for meal prep! Sweet potatoes and ground beef get dolloped with a creamy high protein street corn style dip that is bonkers delicious.

Detox Crockpot Lentil Soup – a clean and simple soup made with onions, garlic, carrots, olive oil, squash, and LENTILS! Super healthy and easy to make.

The BEST Grain Bowl! Roasted root vegetables, earthy grains, dried fruit, dark leafy greens, buttery goat cheese, and lusciously creamy balsamic dressing.

Coconut Curry Salmon! Broiled salmon with a salty-sweet spice rub, creamy coconut curry sauce, and steamy rice to soak it all up.

These tempeh bowls are a true fall favorite! Massaged kale, sweet potatoes, roasty marinated maple-mustard tempeh, crunchy apple, and an unexpected pile of briney sauerkraut.

Lemongrass, ginger, shallot, and the brightness of lime! These broth bowls have got it all – luscious broth, fluffy rice, protein, and fresh herbs.

Saucy shredded chicken, yellow rice, pickled onions, greens, and cilantro pesto on top. It’s a flavor and color delight!

We are living our best bowl life this week. Seasoned sweet potato wedges and chicken meatballs or rotisserie chicken all piled onto a plate with a little puddle of punchy green avocado mojo sauce. Yes, wow, repeat.

#9594. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

Keywords: apple crisp, classic apple crisp, apple crisp recipe, fall dessert
